questions.question: A p-value of 0.02 means...
options: There is a 2% chance that H₀ is true
If H₀ were true, data this extreme would occur about 2% of the time
The effect is 98% likely to be real
questions.explanation: The p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true. It is the probability of data at least this extreme under H₀, not the probability of H₀ itself.

questions.question: You reject H₀ when...
questions.explanation: A p-value at or below the pre-chosen significance level α means the data are too surprising under H₀.

questions.question: A two-tailed z-test gives z = 2.40. What is the p-value (approximately) and the decision at α = 0.05?
questions.explanation: P(Z > 2.40) = 0.0082 in each tail, so the two-tailed p = 0.0164, which is below 0.05. Reject H₀.

questions.question: For z = 1.80, the right-tailed p is 0.0359. What is the two-tailed p?
questions.explanation: The two-tailed p doubles the one-tailed p: 2 × 0.0359 = 0.0719. At α = 0.05 the right-tailed test rejects but the two-tailed test does not.

questions.question: Why must the direction of the test (one- vs two-tailed) be chosen BEFORE looking at the data?
options: Switching to one-tailed after seeing the result halves the p-value and inflates false alarms
questions.explanation: Choosing the direction after the fact is cherry-picking: it makes significance easier to reach and the true false-alarm rate higher than α.

questions.question: A study finds p < 0.001 with n = 50,000 and a difference of 0.02 points on a 100-point scale. The best reading is...
questions.explanation: With a very large n, even trivial differences become 'significant'. The effect size shows whether the difference matters.
